BANGALORE, India (CNN) -- Two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma, an Indian toddler born with four arms and four legs, made her first public appearance Tuesday, a week after surgeons in India successfully removed her additional limbs. Doctors said Lakshmi was recovering well as she appeared Tuesday at a news conference. Lakshmi, wearing a plaster cast on her legs to keep her feet up and her legs together to help her wounds heal, was carried into a news conference Tuesday as her doctors announced she was being released from intensive care. "She is coping very well," lead surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil said. "She is being carried around by her mother and her father." Several of her doctors, all of them smiling, described her recovery over the past week "very steady and good progress," one saying she is "out of the woods" as far as serious medical issues are concerned.  Watch the recovering little girl meet the media » . The operation a week ago lasted 27 hours and involved a team of some 30 surgeons, all specialists in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics, and plastic surgery, working in eight-hour shifts. Lakshmi's extra limbs were part of a conjoined twin which stopped developing in the womb. It had a torso and limbs but no head, and was joined to Lakshmi at the pelvis. Doctors said that without the surgery, Lakshmi would have been unlikely to survive beyond early adolescence. The surgery involved the removal of the extra limbs and the repositioning of Lakshmi's organs. When Lakshmi was born into her poor, rural Indian family, villagers in the remote settlement of Rampur Kodar Katti in the northern state of Bihar believed she was sacred. As news of her birth spread, locals queued for a blessing from the baby. Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named the girl after the Hindu goddess of wealth who has four arms. However, they were forced to keep her in hiding after they were approached by men offering money in exchange for putting their daughter in a circus. The couple, who earn just $1 a day as casual laborers, wanted her to have the operation but were unable to pay for the rare procedure, which had never before been performed in India. After Patil visited the girl in her village from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore, the hospital's foundation agreed to fund the $200,000 operation. Planning for the surgery took a month, Patil said, and Lakshmi spent that month in the hospital. Many villagers, however, remained opposed to surgery and were planning to erect a temple to Lakshmi, whom they still revere as sacred. E-mail to a friend .

The condition, known as ischiopagus, is extraordinarily rare. Doctors said her case was especially unusual and complex because of the way the two bodies were fused.

## The Operation

A team of roughly 30 surgeons and specialists carried out the operation, which lasted more than 24 hours. The procedure involved separating the fused spines, reorganizing internal organs, and reconstructing Lakshmi's pelvis.

Her father said the family had struggled to afford medical care, and the hospital agreed to perform the operation for free, aided by a charitable trust.

# Girl Born with Eight Limbs Undergoes Life-Changing Surgery in Rural India

*A poverty-stricken family's prayers are answered as doctors perform a rare and complex operation on a child some villagers had worshipped as divine.*

---

In a small village in rural India, where the nearest hospital lies hours away by dusty road, a child was born who would soon capture the attention of medical specialists across the country—and stir the deep religious devotion of her community.

The girl, born with what appeared to be eight limbs, arrived into a family of subsistence farmers who could scarcely afford her care. Her condition, doctors would later explain, was the result of an undeveloped parasitic twin—a rare occurrence in which one twin stops developing in the womb but remains attached to the surviving sibling.

## A Rare and Complex Condition

Physicians who examined the child determined that she suffered from a condition sometimes described as heteropagus, or "parasitic twinning." In such cases, an embryo begins to split into identical twins but does not complete the process. One twin develops fully, while the other—lacking a functioning heart or brain—remains partially formed and joined to the host.

The extra limbs, doctors explained, belonged to this undeveloped twin, fused to the surviving child's torso and pelvis. Left uncorrected, the condition posed serious health risks, placing strain on the girl's internal organs and threatening her long-term survival.

"The complexity of these cases cannot be overstated," said one of the surgeons involved. "We are dealing with shared blood supply, delicate spinal connections, and the constant risk of hemorrhage. Every decision carries enormous weight."

## The Weight of Poverty

For the girl's parents, the medical realities were compounded by crushing economic hardship. Her father, a daily-wage laborer, earned only a few dollars for backbreaking work in the fields. The family lived in a modest home with intermittent electricity, and the cost of the surgery—along with travel, medication, and the long hospital stay—was far beyond anything they could imagine paying.

"We are simple people," the father reportedly told those who visited the family. "We did not know how we would save our daughter. We had nothing but our prayers."

The financial burden of complex surgery in India frequently forces poor families into debt or leaves conditions untreated entirely. In this case, the child's plight drew the attention of a charitable hospital and donors who agreed to cover the cost of the operation, offering the family a lifeline they never expected to receive.

## Worshipped as a Goddess

While the family struggled with fear and uncertainty, many in their village saw something else entirely: the divine.

In a region where Hindu tradition venerates deities depicted with multiple arms—goddesses such as Durga and Lakshmi—the child's unusual form led some villagers to believe she was a reincarnation of a goddess. Pilgrims arrived at the family's door to offer prayers, leave gifts, and seek blessings. Some prostrated themselves before the infant, convinced that they stood in the presence of the sacred.

"People came from other villages just to see her," a neighbor recalled. "They believed she was holy. They wanted her to bless their children."

This devotion placed the family in a difficult position. While they were moved by the reverence shown to their daughter, they understood that her condition was a medical matter requiring urgent intervention—not a permanent state of divinity to be preserved.

## The Surgery

The operation, when it finally came, required a large team of surgeons, anesthesiologists, and specialists working in coordinated shifts over many hours. Removing the parasitic limbs demanded meticulous care to protect the child's spine, blood vessels, and organs.

Doctors first conducted extensive imaging studies—CT scans and MRIs—to map the precise connections between the child and her undeveloped twin. Only after understanding exactly how the two were joined could they proceed with the delicate work of separation.

The surgery was described as a success. The medical team removed the additional limbs, and the child was expected to recover and, in time, live a normal life.

"When she woke up and we saw she was stable, there was great relief in the room," one member of the surgical team said. "This is why we do this work."

## A New Beginning

For the family, the operation marked the beginning of a new chapter—one in which their daughter could grow up free from the physical burden she was born with, and perhaps free from the extraordinary expectations placed upon her by those who saw her as sacred.

Whether the villagers who once worshipped her would come to accept her as an ordinary child remained uncertain. But for her parents, the outcome was simple and profound: their daughter would live.

"She is our child," her father said. "That is all we ever wanted—for her to have a life."

---

*Cases of parasitic twinning are exceptionally rare, occurring in roughly one in a million births. Advances in pediatric surgery have made it possible to treat conditions that were once considered untreatable, offering hope to families who might otherwise have had none.*

---

# Born With Eight Limbs, a Girl Named for a Goddess Gets a Second Chance at Life

When Lakshmi Tatma was born in a remote village in the northern Indian state of Bihar, villagers came from miles around—some to marvel, others to worship. The infant girl had been born with four arms and four legs, a rare condition that led many in her deeply religious community to see her as a living embodiment of Lakshmi, the multi-limbed Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, after whom she was named.

But for her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, wonder was tempered by fear. Their daughter's condition was the result of an extraordinarily rare occurrence: an "ischiopagus" conjoined twin. Lakshmi's body had absorbed the underdeveloped, headless twin during pregnancy, leaving her joined at the pelvis to a set of extra limbs and organs. Without surgery, doctors warned, her long-term survival was uncertain.

## A Family's Impossible Choice

The Tatmas were day laborers, poor even by the standards of their rural district. The kind of complex, multi-specialty surgery Lakshmi required was far beyond anything they could ever hope to afford. Compounding their worries, the family lived under the constant pressure of public attention—some wished to venerate the child, while others hoped to exhibit her.

"We just wanted her to be a normal girl," her father said at the time, describing the family's dream that their daughter might one day walk, attend school, and live an ordinary life.

For a family with almost nothing, that dream seemed permanently out of reach.

## A Foundation Steps In

Hope arrived in the form of the Sparsh Hospital in Bangalore and its associated charitable foundation, which agreed to fund and perform the operation at no cost to the family. In November 2007, when Lakshmi was two years old, a team of more than 30 surgeons undertook a marathon procedure that lasted around 27 hours.

The operation was staggering in its complexity. Surgeons had to separate the shared organs, reconstruct Lakshmi's pelvis, and remove the additional limbs—all while protecting the young child's fragile, developing body. The medical team, led by pediatric surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil, described the case as one of the most challenging they had ever encountered.

When it was over, the operation was declared a success.

## From Miracle to Girl

In the years that followed, Lakshmi—once carried through her village as a divine figure—began the slow work of simply being a child. She learned to sit, then stand, then walk, undergoing physiotherapy to strengthen a body that had been dramatically reconfigured.

Her story captured attention around the world, not only for its medical drama but for what it represented: a poor family, unable to help their own child, lifted up by the generosity of strangers and the skill of doctors willing to donate their expertise.

For the Tatmas, the outcome was everything they had prayed for. Their daughter, named for a goddess, had been given the chance to live an ordinary life—a gift that, to them, felt nothing short of divine.

---

*Lakshmi Tatma's case remains one of the most remarkable examples of successful surgical intervention for conjoined twins, and a lasting reminder of the difference charitable medical care can make in the lives of families who have nowhere else to turn.*
